document.title: Comments of Solar Energy Industries Association in response to FERC's 02/20/2025 Order Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act et al

pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al.  
 
 
 
 Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities   
 
 
            AD24-11-000  
 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, L.L.C.   
 
 
 
 
EL25-20-000 
 
          v.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
          (consolidated) 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
COMMENTS OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION 
Maintaining U.S. leadership in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is essential for our national 
security and economic growth.1 To maintain leadership in the industry though, the U.S. needs to 
provide for the rapid development of the data center infrastructure necessary to support AI 
growth. Hyper scalers, utilities, Regional Transmission Organizations, developers, state 
regulators, and the Commission each play a critical role in supporting that infrastructure and its 
significant power demands. And each one of these stakeholders must work expeditiously to 
remove the barriers to that development and provide regulatory certainty.2 
SEIA submits these comments in response to the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order 
Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other 
Proceedings and PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s March 24, 2025 Answer to that Show Cause 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078, Phillips Dissenting, at P 3 (2024) (“Susquehanna ISA Order”); 
Executive Order 14179, “Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence” (Jan. 23, 2025).  
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,025 at P 30, n.106 (2025) (“Susquehanna ISA Rehearing Order”) 
(“We fully intend to act as expeditiously as possible to address those issues, as we know how important it is to 
investors, utilities, and all interested parties to have regulatory certainty.”).

2 
 
Order.3 In the Show Cause Order, the Commission seeks comment on whether the PJM Tariff 
addresses, with sufficient clarity or consistency, the rates, terms, and conditions of service that 
apply to co-location arrangements between large loads and generating facilities. Co-located load 
arrangements are increasingly common in PJM,4 because they help address the large power 
demands of AI infrastructure and new manufacturing.5 However, the PJM Tariff lacks the clarity 
necessary to allow for these kinds of arrangements. In its response to the Show Cause Order, 
PJM presents eight options, three of which are currently in its Tariff. PJM’s answer provides the 
framework for the Commission to direct Tariff changes that will clearly provide for the rates, 
terms, and conditions of co-location agreements.  
SEIA urges the Commission to direct PJM to develop Tariff language implementing the 
five new options for co-location arrangement. As PJM already notes, its options are not mutually 
exclusive.6 Nor should they be. PJM, and the Commission, should provide clear rules for co-
location and provide flexibility and regulatory certainty to accommodate different arrangements. 
Additionally, with respect to PJM’s Option 6, the Bring-your-own Generation option, the 
Commission should direct PJM to create a process by which it would expedite the 
interconnection of generation being used exclusively to serve large load customers through a co-
location arrangement. 
 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”); Answer of PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49 et al. (March 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”). 
4 See, e.g., Docket No. ER24-2172, et al.; EL24-149-000. 
5 Commissioner Led Technical Conference Regarding Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. 
AD24-11, Transcript at 7-9 (Nov. 1, 2024) (“Technical Conference Transcript”) (opening statements of then-Chair 
Phillips); Id. at 16-17 (opening statements of Commissioner See). 
6 PJM Answer at 5 (“Further, identified options are not mutually exclusive, as it is possible several of the options 
may be used seriatim or concurrently.”).

3 
 
I. 
COMMENTS  
A. 
The Commission must base costs on grid use and should accommodate both 
front of the meter and behind the meter load arrangements when setting 
those costs. 
The transmission and ancillary service costs must reflect the benefits the co-located load 
arrangement receives from the grid.7 The type of benefits received will depend on the specific 
co-location arrangement.8 As SEIA noted in our post-technical conference comments, some 
arrangements can be completely islanded from the grid and bear the risk of going offline.9 Others 
cannot take such a risk. Some large loads are flexible and can respond to utility price signals and 
demand response programs. Each arrangement “is going to be a snowflake . . . they are going to 
have their own design, their own concerns, their own issues, their own configurations that they 
would like to meet.”10  
Despite the variety of potential arrangements, PJM’s Tariff lacks any mechanism to 
determine which transmission service classification—and corresponding cost allocation—applies 
to each co-location arrangement. Although PJM prefers large loads to be considered network 
load, in front of the meter,11 two of the options would allow for load to be considered behind the 
meter.12 
 
7 See Show Cause Order at P 77 (questioning whether Network Integration Transmission Service is the appropriate 
transmission service for all co-location arrangements or that such service would be consistent with cost causation 
principle.). 
8 Clean Energy Buyers Association Pre-filed comments at 5, Docket No. AD24-11; Talen Energy Pre-filed 
Comments at 1-3, Docket No. AD24-11 (“Talen has been . . . safely operating co-located loads for over 18 
months.”).   
9 See Post-Workshop Comments of the Solar Energy Industries Association, at 4, Docket No. AD24-11 (Dec. 9, 
2024). 
10 Technical Conference Transcript at 61 (statement of Aubrey Johnson, Vice President, System & Resource 
Planning, Midcontinent Independent System Operator).   
11 PJM Answer at 38. 
12 See PJM Answer at 13-15.

4 
 
SEIA does not take a position on whether the large load should be considered front of the 
meter or behind the meter and urges the Commission to refrain from mandating one network 
configuration over the other. As the Commission itself recognized, “[t]he record demonstrates 
that different co-location arrangements are likely to use or benefit from the transmission system 
in different ways depending on how they are configured and, moreover, that those different 
configurations will themselves likely have different impacts on the transmission system.”13 There 
are trade-offs in each model and no single model can address the full spectrum of technical 
considerations across the variety of co-location proposals. The Commission should maintain both 
pathways so that each project can select the configuration best suited to its commercial structure 
and reliability needs. As the Commission observes, “there is no clear record before us that 
Network Integration Transmission Service is the appropriate transmission service for all co-
location arrangements or that such service would be consistent with the cost causation principle 
… for such arrangements.”14  
The Commission should refrain from preferencing a particular Network configuration. 
Beyond technical and market considerations, the importance of data-center growth to U.S. 
economic competitiveness and national security reinforces the need for regulatory neutrality. As 
then-Chairman Phillips observed, “data centers…are national resources, with generational 
significance, and vast national security and national economic consequences. They belong in the 
United States, and…this agency should be doing [its] very best to nurture and foster their 
development.”15 Preferential treatment of one network configuration would constrict, rather than 
 
13 Show Cause Order at P 76; see also Atlantic City Electric Co., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,109 (2025) (rejecting Tariff 
revisions proposing to charge all co-located load based on a gross load basis). 
14 Show Cause Order at P 77. 
15 Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11, November 1, 2024, Technical 
Conference, Tr. at 8. (Technical Conference).

5 
 
foster, domestic development. Policymakers across the spectrum agree that data-center 
expansion is too vital to be hamstrung by rigid Network mandates. The Commission should 
affirm that each customer can select the configuration that best meets its needs.  
B. 
The Commission should direct PJM to create processes in its Tariff to 
effectuate Options 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8. 
1. 
The PJM Tariff lacks provisions to address the co-location of large loads 
and generation. 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission found that the PJM Tariff  “appears to be 
unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential because it does not contain 
provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of 
service that apply to co-location arrangements.”16 Despite statements from PJM,17 and the PJM 
Indicated Transmission Owners,18 the PJM Tariff does not address with “clarity or consistency 
the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements.”19  
While PJM presents three options that are currently in its Tariff, only one of those options 
explicitly provides for co-location. Option 1, Load with a separate Point of Interconnection that 
is Network Load, explicitly provides that the load and generation are not co-located.20 Though 
presented as a large load co-location option for the Commission to consider,21 it does not meet 
PJM’s definition of co-located load because the load and generation are behind separate Points of 
Interconnection.22 Similarly, Option 2, Co-located load that is at the same Point of 
 
16 Show Cause Order at P 74. 
17 PJM Answer at 4, 32. 
18 Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners to the Order Instituting the Proceeding Under Section 206 of 
the Federal Power Act at 12 (March 24, 2025) (“Indicated TOs Answer”). 
19 Show Cause Order at 87. 
20 PJM Answer at 9 (“This option is where the load is network load and generation is a capacity resource and they 
are not electrically co-located.”). 
21 PJM Answer at 5. 
22 See PJM, PJM Guidance on Co-Located Load at 1 (March 22, 2024) (updated April 17, 2024), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/pjm-guidance-on-co-located-load.pdf 
(Guidance Document); see also Show Cause Order at P 3.

6 
 
Interconnection but separately metered, allows the load and generation to be behind the same 
point of interconnection, but each is metered separately.23 Effectively, this treats the load and 
generation as distinct from each other. 
Option 3, Existing Behind the Meter Generation (BTMG) where the load is the customer, 
reflects PJM’s existing BTMG rules where the load is the primary customer and nets with 
BTMG.24 Many of the existing co-location arrangements in PJM operate under this arrangement. 
It is an option under the existing Tariff, but as PJM admits, it was not designed for the co-
location needs of hyper-scalers.25  The use of this option is limited to 2,000 megawatts (MW), of 
which about 1,300 MW are already used.26 This is far short of the 40 GWs of data center 
contracts announced in just the Dominion service territory alone.27 
The existing options under the PJM Tariff do not provide for rates, terms, and conditions 
of service that apply to the co-location arrangements at issue in this proceeding, the 
arrangements needed to serve large loads. While Options 1 and 2 may work for some large loads 
and generation and should remain available, neither one qualifies as a co-location arrangement. 
Without a clear set of rules to interconnect and allocate the transmission and ancillary services 
costs of co-location arrangements between large load and generation, the PJM Tariff is unjust, 
unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.28  
 
23 PJM Answer at 11. 
24 Id. 
25 PJM Answer at 13, n. 5. 
26 Id. 
27 See Around the Corner: The Promise, Uncertainty and Unparalleled Risk of Data Center Load, RTO Insider, April 
20, 2025, https://www.rtoinsider.com/103016-around-the-corner-promise-uncertainty-unparalleled-risk-data-center-
load/. 
28 See Show Cause Order at P 75.

7 
 
2. 
The new options provided in PJM’s Answer would result in just and 
reasonable rates, terms, and conditions for co-location of large load and 
generation. 
In its Answer, PJM presented five “potential options that have been proposed by others or 
developed by PJM in response to issues raised in the various predecessor co-located load 
proceedings.”29 The Commission should direct PJM to develop and file Tariff revisions to 
implement each of these five options. 
The November Technical Conference demonstrated that large loads come in different 
shapes and sizes.30 In the Show Cause Order, the Commission recognized that “The record 
demonstrates that different co-location arrangements are likely to use or benefit from the 
transmission system in different ways depending on how they are configured and, moreover, that 
those different configurations will themselves likely have different impacts on the transmission 
system.”31 As the Indicated Transmission Owners recognized, there is an “evolving co-location 
configuration.”32  
This proceeding has only just scratched the surface of the technical capabilities of data 
centers when it comes to energy needs, load flexibility, and demand reduction. This is, in part, 
because the market does not yet “know yet what types of load flexibility we're going to fully see 
from data centers.”33 The technology is constantly evolving and may result in significant power 
savings for both new and existing data centers.34 Researchers from the Nicholas Institute at Duke 
 
29 PJM Answer at 5. 
30 See November Technical Conference Transcript, supra note 11.  
31 Show Cause Order at P 76. 
32 Indicated TOs Answer at 12; see also Technical Conference Transcript at 57, statement of Commissioner See 
(“…but as so many of you have said, this is an area where details matter, and we're seeing fast innovation and 
changes here.”). 
33 Technical Conference Transcript at 149. 
34 How liquid cooling can address AI's water crisis in data centers, Data Center Dynamics (Nov. 4, 2024), 
https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/opinions/how-liquid-cooling-can-address-ais-water-crisis-in-data-centers/ 
(“In addition to reducing water usage, liquid cooling offers a major boost to energy efficiency. … Many existing 
data centers are also working on liquid cooling retrofits for at least parts of their data centers.”).

8 
 
University recently stated that “A variety of recent developments in computational load profiles, 
operational capabilities, and broader market conditions, however, suggest that a new phase of 
opportunity and necessity is emerging.”35 The training of the neural networks used to power large 
language models and other machine learning algorithms is deferrable, meaning that these 
processes could shift to periods of lower grid demand.36 These processes could also be shifted to 
other data centers on the grid, to areas where there is less grid demand or more renewable energy 
available.37 These emerging capabilities, as well as the ability for a large load customer to bring 
its own generation in an expedited manner, make it so that certain customers may not need the 
full suite of grid services, or may accept the risk of not having that full suite of services available 
to them. And, to support these solutions, the underlying rate designs should encourage “flexible 
load customers to be able to . . . move consumption away from peak periods.”38  
The potential for load flexibility necessitates “regulatory flexibility.”39 Regulatory 
flexibility, in this context, means that the Commission requires PJM to implement “optionality so 
that customers have the ability to select the best configuration for their particular circumstances 
and needs.”40 Co-located loads with the ability to curtail or shift demand in coordination with 
generator output or grid constraints should be treated differently than firm grid-dependent load, 
as these loads would be capable of reducing their demand on the grid. This is a fact that PJM’s 
earlier guidance on co-location recognized.41 The Commission must do all it can to ensure the 
 
35 Duke University’s Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability, Rethinking Load Growth: 
Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads at 11, Feb. 2025, 
www.nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/publications (emphasis added).  
36 Id. 
37 Id. 
38 Technical Conference Transcript, at 125, comments of Pallas LeeVanSchaick. 
39 Susquehanna ISA Order, Phillips, Chairman, dissenting statement at P 3. 
40 Response of Public Service Electric and Gas Company at 20; see also Technical Conference Transcript at 90, 124. 
41 Show Cause Order at P 4 (citing Guidance Document at 2) (“certain parties may wish to pursue a co-location 
arrangement without procuring applicable firm transmission service, in which case the load is not designated as 
Network Load.”).

9 
 
United States “nurture and foster” the development of AI infrastructure.42 Regulatory flexibility 
is critical to “support that development.”43  
The five new options presented by PJM in its answer provide a path for the Commission 
to exercise that “regulatory flexibility.” The Commission should direct PJM to develop and file 
the necessary Tariff language to implement each of these options.44  
C. 
The Commission should direct PJM to fast-track new generation that would 
come online via co-location agreements. 
While making progress, PJM is still in the process of transitioning its backlogged serial 
queue to the new cluster study process. It has been well established throughout this proceeding, 
and several other proceedings, that the addition of large loads to the PJM system is outpacing the 
addition of the new resources needed to serve that new load.45 Several comments in this 
proceeding have noted that when new large loads sought to co-locate behind the meter of 
existing generation, there could be resource adequacy issues.46 The Commission echoed these 
potential concerns in the Show Cause Order.47 
 
42 Technical Conference Transcript at 8. 
43 Technical Conference Transcript at 20. 
44 See PJM Answer at 5 (“Each new option outlined herein is conceptual and would benefit from continued input 
from stakeholders, Commission guidance, and a deadline for submission of any such proposals either in the context 
of a section 205 filing or in this docket.”). 
45 Technical Conference Transcript at 165 (statements of D.C. Public Service Commission Chairman Emile C. 
Thompson); NERC 2024 Long-Term Reliability Assessment, at 24 (Dec. 2024) (“The added resource capacity on 
the BPS over the past year fell short of industry’s projections, raising concerns that demand growth has the potential 
to outpace supply resources.”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Tariff Revisions for Reliability Resource Initiative, at 
2, Docket No. ER25-712 (Dec. 13, 2025); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposed Tariff Amendments for Surplus 
Interconnection Service, at 5, Docket No. ER26-778 (Dec. 20, 2024) (PJM Surplus Filing). 
46 See Show Cause Order at PP 62-64 (summarizing the resource adequacy concerns in the proceedings); Technical 
Conference Transcript at 111 (statement of PJM Independent Market Monitor, Joe Bowering). 
47 Show Cause Order at P 84.

10 
 
 One way to address these concerns is to “figure out ways to bring new gen[eration] 
online.”48 PJM’s Option 6 provides the basis to do exactly that.49 Option 6 “offers a potentially 
faster interconnection path for generation resources supporting co-located loads.”50 The 
Commission should direct PJM to modify this option to implement an expedited co-located 
interconnection process, separate from the queue, to determine whether the interconnection 
request for the co-located generation would require new Network Upgrades.  
Under this model, PJM would study the generator, whether utility owned or owned by an 
independent power producer, similar to how it would study surplus service requests, in order to 
determine whether any new Network Upgrades would be needed to facilitate the interconnection 
request.51 One assumption of this co-location interconnection study would be that the resources 
using this interconnection option would supply their entire output to the co-located load, and 
would not be exporting to the grid and therefore these arrangements should be exempt from 
traditional Network Upgrade triggers or full deliverability requirements.  
This process would be analogous to the widely-supported surplus interconnection 
service.52 In Order No. 845, the Commission stated that “surplus interconnection service is 
created because generating facilities may not operate at full capacity at all times.”53 Under a co-
located interconnection process, the generating facility may be operating at full capacity, 
however, that capacity would never exceed the requirements of the co-located load, and therefore 
 
48 Technical Conference Transcript at 112 (statement of PJM Independent Market Monitor, Joe Bowering); see also 
SEIA Comments in Docket No. AD24-11. 
49 SEIA recognizes that this option would also “be open for existing generation that could serve the energy needs of 
the large loads so long as the generator would still be available to PJM as a Capacity Resource if it clears in the 
capacity market.” The discussion here is focused solely on the ability to bring new resources onto the grid. 
50 PJM Answer at 17. 
51 See PJM Tariff, Subpart E, Section 414(B), Surplus Interconnection Study. 
52 See Reform of Generator Interconnection Procedures and Agreements, Order No. 845, 163 FERC ¶ 61,043 at P 
467 (2018) (“Order No. 845”), reh’g denied & clarification granted, Order No. 845-A, 166 FERC ¶ 61,137 at P 138 
(“Order No. 845-A”), order on reh’g & clarification, Order No. 845-B, 168 FERC ¶ 61,092 (2019).  
53 Order No. 845 at P 468.

11 
 
would not require transmission service to export to the grid.54 Similar to surplus interconnection 
service, co-located interconnection service would not be queue jumping because the co-located 
resources would not be competing for Network Upgrades.55 
The purpose of co-located interconnection service is twofold. First, this service would 
help address the “rapid tightening of supply and demand” that PJM has highlighted in several 
filings.56 Bringing new supply online faster will alleviate some of the demand pressures on the 
PJM system. Second, fast tracking new generation may also help prevent transmission system 
overbuild. Utilities include planned data centers in their load projections and transmission 
planning. The utility may begin incurring transmission costs to accommodate that load and those 
costs may end up stranded if the data center project is cancelled and the load does not show up.57 
By allowing co-located generation to come online along with the large loads, the grid impact of 
the large load would likely be reduced, which would reduce the need to plan for Network 
Upgrades. The Commission should direct PJM to create a fast-track co-location interconnection 
process to ensure that new generation is timely, reliable, and avoids unnecessary transmission 
overbuild.  
 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
The Commission finds itself in a critical position with respect to how the U.S. will 
maintain its leadership in AI technology. Power, and lots of it, is needed to supply AI 
 
54 It may still be possible under a co-location interconnection process for the load to require transmission service. 
55 See Order No. 845 at P 487. If the co-located interconnection study reveals that network upgrades are necessary, 
then the co-located interconnection request would be deemed ineligible for this interconnection service. 
56 See PJM Surplus Filing at 5. 
57 See Post-Technical Conference Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. at 5-6, Docket No. AD24-11 (Dec. 9, 2024); 
Post-Technical Conference Comments of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association at 3, Docket No. 
AD24-11 (Dec. 9, 2024); Technical Conference Transcript at 51 (statement of Aaron Tinjum, the Data Center 
Coalition).

12 
 
infrastructure. But to provide that power, market participants need clear, and flexible rules 
regarding the co-location of large load generation. PJM has provided the Commission with a 
framework for doing that. SEIA urges the Commission to act expeditiously in directing PJM to 
further define and develop that framework into workable Tariff provisions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,  
 
Melissa Alfano   
Senior Director of Energy Markets and Counsel   
Greg Giunta   
Manager of Regulatory Affairs and Counsel  
Solar Energy Industries Association
